summary: Specifies the combinations of security mechanisms that are required and recommended in LDAP implementations for authentication. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: This says which ways of proving who you are an LDAP directory must accept, and which are recommended, so different programs can log in to each other.

subtitle: Which ways of proving identity every LDAPv3 directory must support, and how to combine them with TLS.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 offers a rich set of security functions, but if every implementation picks its own, clients and servers may share no common way to authenticate, or fall back on cleartext passwords.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets a minimum: anonymous access, DIGEST-MD5 for password logins, and, for protected sessions, Start TLS combined with a simple password bind or a client certificate through SASL EXTERNAL.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513 and updated by RFC 3377, so it is no longer the current definition of LDAP authentication.

today: RFC 2829 was a Proposed Standard and is obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513. It was also updated by RFC 3377. Use the newer documents for current LDAP authentication rules.

sections.title: Why a Minimum Security Set
sections.content:
LDAP version 3 is an access protocol for directories. It can search, fetch and change directory content, and it offers a rich set of security functions. For those functions to be interoperable, the RFC says there has to be a minimum subset common to all implementations that claim LDAPv3 conformance.

It lists seven basic threats, from unauthorized reads and modifications to denial of service and spoofing of the directory. Threats (1), (4), (5) and (6) come from hostile clients. Threats (2), (3) and (7) come from hostile agents on the path, or posing as a server. The available defences are SASL authentication, access control, TLS or SASL integrity and encryption layers, administrative resource limits and server authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: If every directory used its own secret handshake, nobody could get in anywhere. This document picks a few handshakes that everyone must know.

sections.title: Identities and Access Control
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. Authentication credentials are the evidence one party supplies to assert its identity, such as X.509 certificates, Kerberos tickets or a simple identity and password pair. The authentication identity is the name presented in a credential.

An authorization identity is the name of the user or other entity on whose behalf operations are performed. It is often the same as the authentication identity but may differ. SASL lets a proxy server authenticate with its own credentials while requesting the privileges of the identity it is proxying. Servers decide what to allow using access control factors such as source IP address, encryption strength, the type of operation or time of day.
sections.plainLanguage: Showing your library card proves who you are. What you are allowed to borrow is a separate question, and sometimes a parent borrows on a child's behalf.

sections.title: Required Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC argues that letting implementations pick and choose would lead to clients that support nothing the server supports, or only cleartext passwords. So it sets conformance requirements:

  • A read-only public directory can use anonymous authentication.
  • Implementations offering password-based access MUST support the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism. It protects against passive eavesdropping but not against active intermediary attacks.
  • For session protection plus authentication, use the Start TLS operation with either the simple bind or SASL EXTERNAL. Implementations SHOULD support a password login and a certificate login this way.

After TLS or a SASL security layer is negotiated, the client MUST discard everything it learned about the server beforehand. It SHOULD fetch supportedSASLMechanisms before and after a SASL security layer and check that the value has not changed, which detects an attacker stripping mechanisms out of the list.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must at least know one safe way to prove who they are. If you want to whisper too, you switch to a locked room first and then show your ID.

sections.title: Anonymous, Password and Certificate Logins
sections.content:
Anonymous: implementations MUST support it. A client that has not completed a bind is anonymous, and it may also ask for it with a zero-length OCTET STRING in a simple bind. Servers SHOULD let an anonymous client read the supportedSASLMechanisms attribute of the root DSE.

Password with DIGEST-MD5: the client first sends a bind with version 3, the sasl choice, mechanism name DIGEST-MD5 and no credentials. The server answers saslBindInProgress with a challenge. The client sends a second bind with its digest response and the service type ldap, and the server replies with success or an error.

Simple bind under TLS: after Start TLS gives a ciphersuite with confidentiality, the client sends a bind with version 3, the user's entry name and a password. The server compares it for case-sensitive equality with each userPassword value, answering success or invalidCredentials.

Certificate: the server MUST request a certificate during TLS and verify it is valid, and the client MUST prove it holds the private key. Afterwards the client sends a bind with the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism. If no TLS session or other external credentials exist, that bind MUST fail with inappropriateAuthentication.
sections.plainLanguage: You can walk in as a guest, whisper a password through a locked door, or show an ID card signed by someone the guard trusts.

sections.title: Authorization Identity Format and Ciphersuites
sections.content:
The authorization identity travels in the SASL credentials of the bind. It is a UTF-8 string in one of two forms: dn: followed by a distinguished name, or u: followed by an unspecified user id. Servers that store credentials in the directory MUST support the dn: form. A u: id MUST NOT be assumed to be globally unique.

Section 10 lists TLS ciphersuites. The NULL suites such as TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL MUST NOT be used to protect passwords or data. Export-grade suites, which the RFC says could be cracked in under a week of CPU time on a standard CPU in 1997, call for careful consideration. Anonymous Diffie-Hellman suites SHOULD NOT protect sensitive data because they allow man-in-the-middle attacks. Any implementation supporting TLS MUST support TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say who you are by full name or by a nickname the guard knows. Some locks are too weak to trust, so the rules ban the worst ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that mandatory security is important and that session encryption is required when snooping is a problem. Servers are encouraged to prevent modifications by anonymous users, and may time out idle connections and return unwillingToPerform instead of doing costly work for unauthorized clients.

A connection without Start TLS or a suitable SASL integrity and encryption layer is open to man-in-the-middle attacks that view and modify information in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: If you talk in the open, anyone in the hallway can listen or change your note. Switch to a private room when the message matters.
